name: Spervogel
credit: Spervogel, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Spervogel is the name given to two itinerant poets of the later twelfth century, distinguished by scholars as Spervogel I and Spervogel II, whose short moral and proverbial stanzas are among the oldest German Spruchdichtung.
Eight songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), five marked as Spervogel I and three as Spervogel II as in his book.

poems.title: Testament
poems.author: Spervogel
poems.text:
I tell you this, dear sons of mine,
For you there grows not corn nor wine;
You must not think to get from me
Lands to own or hold in fee.
Now speed you God in Heaven
And give you grace and happiness!
To Frut of Denmark fortune fair was given.

poems.title: The Hedgehog
poems.author: Spervogel
poems.text:
What the hedgehog said is known:
"There's nought like quarters of one's own."
Kerling, build a house and store
All thy gear within the door!
The lords are all grown greedy.
Whoever has not hearth and home,
How often is he hard bestead and needy!

poems.title: Host and Guest
poems.author: Spervogel
poems.text:
Be the weather what it may,
The guest must rise at break of day.
Dry-shod oft the host may sit,
When the guest must up and quit
The quarters where he's staying.
Whoe'er in his old age would be
A host, must start in youth without delaying!

poems.title: Pains of Hell
poems.author: Spervogel
poems.text:
Great distress there is in hell:
Whosoever there doth dwell
Never sees the light of sun,
Neither aid from the moon
Or the shining stars is given.
Nay, all he sees doth vex him sore:
In sooth, he then would gladly be in Heaven!

poems.title: Praise ye Him!
poems.author: Spervogel
poems.text:
All roots of wood and wold
And hidden veins of gold
And deeps of land and sea,
Lord, they all are known to Thee;
In Thy hand they lie duly.
All the heavenly host above
Hath not the power to tell Thy praises fully.

poems.title: Ill-Luck
poems.author: Spervogel
poems.text:
Ill-luck is mine, and that hath often made me grieve:
Thus, ere I drunk a drop, a lake I had to leave,
From which a cool stream took its course
And flowed along with mighty force.
Thereat full many slaked their thirst and for the draught felt better.
How oft soe'er I dipped my bowl, its lip grew never wetter!

poems.title: The Lot of All
poems.author: Spervogel
poems.text:
This blade of straw we praise, for produce it hath borne.
The season hath been fair and plentiful of corn,
And glad thereat the world hath been.
Where could a fairer straw be seen?
With plenteous store the rich man's barns and coffers it supplieth.
Then, when it once hath done its part, rotten and foul it lieth.

poems.title: Clothed in Honour
poems.author: Spervogel
poems.text:
Though a chaste woman may not wear a costly dress,
Full sure am I, she's clad in her own worthiness,
So that in brave attire she goes,
Even as the sun at morning shows
His bright beams pure and clear. A guileful dame may wear upon her
As costly raiment as she will, scant is her share of honour.
